HEADLINE: Japan cuts interest rates below zero
INTRO: In a desperate bid to invigorate its sluggish economy the Bank of Japan took financial markets by surprise on Friday when it said it would push interest rates below zero, a move that will weaken the yen and add to global currency tensions especially with China.
TEXT:
In a desperate bid to invigorate its sluggish economy the Bank of Japan took financial markets by surprise on Friday when it said it would push interest rates below zero, a move that will weaken the yen and add to global currency tensions especially with China.

Any commercial bank that now chooses to leave money on deposit at the central bank will be charged a rate of minus 0.1 per cent, when previously they would earn plus 0.1 per cent.

The BoJ wants to make it difficult for banks to hoard any cash and by charging them they hope the banks will get more aggressive in their lending to business.

"This is just yet another way of adding stimulus to the economy that should weaken the yen and help anyone who was worried about a crash in sharemarkets. This should help push equity markets up," National Australia Bank's chief economist Alan Oster said.

Traders reacted quickly to the decision by selling the yen and pushing up Japanese stocks, while the yield on the key 10-year Japanese government bond fell to 0.175 per cent, an all-time low.

The major S&P ASX 200 index closed up 29.3 to 5005.5 on Friday. The Nikkei, which earlier this month dipped into a bear market, closed up 2.8 per cent. The major index has posted gains for the second consecutive week but is still down 5.5 per cent in 2016. The move in the yen against the greenback was also swift with one US dollar now buying 121.49 yen, compared to 118.6 before the announcement.

The Australian dollar also gained against the yen. One $A now buys 86.2 yen compared to 84 yen previously.

The bold move comes as low inflation, a falling oil price and the worst start to a year on Wall Street on record has caused violent moves in financial markets that could upset Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's plan to grow the economy and get inflation to 2 per cent.

While it's the first time the BoJ has used the policy, some other key European central banks, including Sweden, Denmark, and Switzerland have already cut their key interest rates below zero in a bid to stimulate their economy.

Denmark has also used negative interest rates to protect its currency's peg to the euro while it has been used by some banks to get foreigners to move their money and put it somewhere else. But it's not orthodox central banking, smells of desperation and can cause angst in financial markets as traders worry about another bout of currency wars.

Julian Evans-Pritchard from Capital Economics said the Chinese yuan was likely to weaken further following the move, but stopped short of calling the start of a region-wide currency war. "Weakness in the yen makes it more likely we will see further falls in the yuan ," he said from Singapore.

Capital is forecasting the yuan to hit 6.8 to the US dollar by the end of this year, compared to 6.57 currently.

But he does not believe the yuan will weaken in Trade Weighted Terms (against a basket of currencies), which should avert a chain reaction of competitive devaluations across the region.

"The yuan has been stable in trade weighted terms over the last six months," he said. "So until you see a significant depreciation of the yuan in trade weighted terms I don't think you can call the start of a currency war. I don't think you will see countries fighting to weaken their currencies against each other. It's more a passive devaluation drive by the US dollar's strength"

The decision wasn't straight forward and the board was spilt but it got over the line with a 5-4 majority.

It starts on February 16, and was announced on Friday at the conclusion of a two-day policy meeting. Financial markets were expecting some sort of news around asset purchases but in the end the BoJ decided not to expand its quantitative easing programme beyond the current level of buying 80 trillion of assets in yen each year. The bank also said "It will cut the interest rate further into negative territory if judged necessary".

"The rate cut comes out of the blue, and is another shock tactic from the BoJ," said Gregg Gibbs, an independent currency analyst.

Ironically , as the board met on Friday investors were greeted with the latest economic report and it wasn't good. Industrial production was down 1.4 per cent in December, compared with forecasts of a 0.3 per cent fall, while the renewed fall in oil prices also weighed on inflation.

The report implies the BoJ's 2 per cent inflation target — a major part of Mr Abe's economic package — is still way out of reach.

HEADLINE: Australia's rebrand woos investors
INTRO: Australia's pitch to reinvent itself in the eyes of global investors received a vote of confidence from asset manager Putnam Investments, which says Australia has shaken its reputation as a resources-dependent economy.
TEXT:
Australia's pitch to reinvent itself in the eyes of global investors received a vote of confidence from asset manager Putnam Investments, which says Australia has shaken its reputation as a resources-dependent economy.

Senior government ministers, including Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull, top regulators, representatives of the Reserve Bank of Australia and executives from BHP Billiton, Transurban and other big companies briefed international fund managers in Sydney on Friday at an event staged by Citigroup in an effort to rehabilitate Australia's investment image. This comes in the wake of China's slowdown and the commodity price collapse which has undermined confidence in Australia as an investment destination.

Darren Jaroch, a portfolio manager at the $200 billion Boston-based Putnam, said he left more at ease with the outlook for Australia. "The popular perception outside of Australia particularly from US fund managers has been this economy that has been so linked with basic materials and China, both of which are top of mind," he told AFR Weekend. "I'm feeling much more comfortable with what I'm seeing in Australia now than I was just six months ago.

"Whether it's Chinese tourism, there are other trade relationships with China that don't involve iron ore or LNG for that matter."

He pointed to the duty-free shopping displays at Sydney Airport targeted at China's growing ranks of international travellers and their preference for expensive cognac over cheaper liquors.

"That is fascinating because they've got it down to a science," he said.

Mr Turnbull told the investors Australia was unrivalled for having 25 years of unbroken growth while Treasurer Scott Morrison assured them the government's triple-A credit rating was sound and the slowdown in China was expected.

Trade Minister Andrew Robb, who was instrumental in bringing the political leaders, regulators and corporate leaders into the Sydney Opera House's Utzon Room for one day, emphasised Australia's bipartisan policy reform, stable political environment and "low levels of government debt".

The message of political unity at the forum was at odds with the daily rhetoric between the Coalition and Labor but Mr Robb said it was important to show Australia had a common sense approach to economic reform.

"It is impossible to gild the lily because these are not people you can fool with a few glib lines," Mr Robb said.

Guests at the invitation-only meeting - which government and business representatives hope to make an annual event dubbed the A50 Australian Economic Forum - said they were surprised by the frank discussion with Australia's regulators, which have the power to approve or reject some of the biggest deals involving international investors.

Ryan Stork, head of Asia-Pacific for BlackRock, saw "a pivot" in Australia's growth "to service sectors, be it food, be it healthcare, be it education and obviously tourism as well".

Australian Competition and Consumer Commission chairman Rod Sims told the audience his agency had such a wide range of responsibilities that "what we don't have is a lot of time on our hands".

"I guess they would have seen that a positive from their point of view," Mr Sims said outside the forum.

Mr Sims also talked about the biggest international mergers currently attracting the regulator's attention including Halliburton's $US35 billion acquisition of oil exploration services business Baker Hughes and Iron Mountain's $2.7 billion takeover bid for Australian company Recall Holdings.

He said logistics company boss John Mullen was in the "wonderful position of having two companies fighting over him" in the $9 billion battle for Asciano between Brookfield Infrastructure and the Qube consortium.

Australian Prudential Regulation Authority chair Wayne Byres said bank would probably have to hold more capital over time, but the increase would be managed in an orderly way.

Treasury secretary John Fraser was on hand to help with the government's sales pitch to international fund managers, whose investments in Australia have fallen to the lowest level in 20 years. "It is these sorts of meetings that provide a great occasion to have a sober discussion not only about the challenges facing Australia but, more importantly, about the opportunities Australia presents to international partners," he said.

HEADLINE: Bank of Japan answers investors' stimulus prayers
INTRO: Investors' prayers for more monetary stimulus to revive swooning markets were answered on Friday afternoon, with the Bank of Japan stunning traders by adding negative interest rates to its huge asset-buying program.
TEXT:
Investors' prayers for more monetary stimulus to revive swooning markets were answered on Friday afternoon, with the Bank of Japan stunning traders by adding negative interest rates to its huge asset-buying program.

The Japanese central bank's decision means that it is now following in the steps of the European Central Bank, as well as central banks in Sweden, Switzerland and Denmark, in charging financial institutions that park large deposits in their vaults.

The BoJ said the move was designed to stop the turbulence in financial markets from undermining Japanese business confidence and reviving the country's "deflationary mindset".

But many analysts believe the move shows that the bank believes its huge bond-buying program - running at ¥80 trillion ($930 billion) a year - is reaching its limits. The huge program has caused the Bank of Japan's balance sheet to balloon to close to 80 per cent of the country's GDP.

The problem for the bank is that January's market turmoil has sparked a flight to safety, and this, combined with the unwind of carry trades, pushed the yen to ¥117 to the US dollar in January, compared with ¥122 to the greenback in December.

The strengthening yen posed a threat to the profits of the big Japanese exporters, which have benefited hugely from the steep drop in the currency in the past three years. And the outlook for lower corporate profits would weigh on the Japanese sharemarket, which has already fallen by just under 10 per cent so far this year.

What's more, a stronger yen reduces the costs of imports, dealing a further blow to the BoJ's hopes of kindling inflationary pressures. Already, the bank has been forced to cut its inflation forecast for the coming financial year to 0.8 per cent from the 1.4 per cent projected only three months ago.

The risk of a continued rise in the yen forced the Bank of Japan to set aside its long-standing resistance to negative interest rates, and to slash the interest rate it pays on reserves that financial institutions hold with the central bank to minus 0.1 per cent.

All the same, the move is not without its risks. Some economists argue that negative interest rates erode the profitability of banks, which can trigger financial instability. What's more, they note, fragile financial institutions are unlikely to want to boost their lending to businesses and households.

But the Japanese central bank is prepared to take the gamble. And the yen's steep decline in the wake of the decision suggests that the BoJ's wager might just pay off.

HEADLINE: Mackenzie's big hope could be history repeating itself
INTRO: A BHP boss is at Broken Hill for the first time in 77 years.
TEXT:
A BHP boss is at Broken Hill for the first time in 77 years.

BHP Billiton might be struggling to find many friends on global markets, but when chief executive Andrew Mackenzie visited the company's birthplace of Broken Hill this week he received a very warm reception.

As pressure mounts on BHP, Broken Hill is the last place you might think Mackenzie should be. But if history is a guide it could bode well for the BHP.

Broken Hill hasn't had a BHP CEO visit since before World War II, although chairman James McNeill and board members visited in 1983.

Back then, like now, BHP was battling a commodity price rout. Mackenzie, who finds himself besieged by an unexpected collapse in the oil price, could be forgiven for hoping for a certain historical symmetry from the last time BHP's big wigs came to town.

Not long after McNeill visited, he helped engineer BHP's acquisition of Utah International from General Electric. The $US2.4 billion cash purchase was unprecedented and not without its critics, with Labor politicians in Australia calling it "absolutely scandalous". Commodity prices, particularly coal, were under pressure, and the purchase price was large.

But the gamble paid off and it was the acquisition that turned BHP from an Australian company into a global one. It made BHP a major coal exporter in Queensland and extended the company's operations into the United States, Brazil, Canada and Chile. It helped make BHP a force in copper by delivering it a controlling stake in the giant mine Escondida.

Indeed, it is arguably the most important moment in the company's history - perhaps aside from the discovery of huge silver, zinc and lead deposits in Broken Hill in 1883 that led to the creation of BHP, which stands for Broken Hill Proprietary, two years later.

Could a similar company-changing deal be just around the corner for Andrew Mackenzie? A transaction that would let him change the conversation from the pain of commodity prices and dividend cuts to smart growth?

It's not impossible and some within BHP think that Mackenzie could be preparing for such a deal. The company has an appetite for mergers and acquisitions in copper and conventional oil as it hunts a bigger presence in both commodities.

Mackenzie wants producing assets and is prepared to buy at a company or a project level. Of course with prices falling, especially in oil, what he is willing to pay has no doubt changed.

Mackenzie gets the chance to at least start the process of changing the conversation in a few weeks when he fronts the company's half-yearly results on February 23. BHP is set to post a statutory loss due in no small part to $US4.9 billion ($6.9 billion) in post-tax write-downs in shale, but investors already know that.

The loudest questions are about its policy on its $US6.6 billion annual progressive dividend policy, and what new capital management direction it will take to better protect its balance sheet.

The company's commitment to its progressive dividend policy - that held the annual dividend would not fall in US dollar terms - looks certain to go.

But Andy Forster, senior investment officer at top 10 BHP shareholder Argo Investments, says BHP's commitment to "protecting our strong balance sheet" indicates it is also likely to cut the interim dividend next month, and the focus will be on by how much and what policy it pursues after that.

Forster says he has confidence that BHP will do what it takes, including cutting capital spending further, to fix the balance sheet.

But the question remains how BHP will adjust to the oil price collapse, and how it repositions itself - and its balance sheet - to deal with the new price reality.

More write-downs in its oil and gas business are likely if it cuts its long-term oil price assumptions.

But cutting its dividend is BHP's big lever. Analysts expect it will halve its interim dividend from US62¢ to US31¢. It can also cut capital spending more deeply, and more productivity gains can boost free cash flow.

If done right, an acquisition, whether it be oil or copper, could go some way to fixing the company's woes and reposition it after years of focusing on productivity to generate growth and shunning M&A.

BHP would be loathe to do a rights issue to shore up the balance sheet, but if it were executed to fund a decent acquisition, that would be a much easier sell to investors.

That's where its London listing, which is being reviewed, would come in handy too.

HEADLINE: Brazilian criticism boggles BHP
INTRO: On Thursday, BHP Billiton's chief executive, Andrew Mackenzie, made a well-intentioned journey to outback Broken Hill, home of the Global Australian's original mother-lode of silver. But should he have been in Brasilia instead?
TEXT:
On Thursday, BHP Billiton's chief executive, Andrew Mackenzie, made a well-intentioned journey to outback Broken Hill, home of the Global Australian's original mother-lode of silver. But should he have been in Brasilia instead?

A few hours after Mackenzie left the Silver City for Sydney, negotiators from BHP and its Brazilian counterpart in global mining, Vale, stepped into a second meeting in just days with a Brazilian government that is publicly determined to bring rapid conclusion to a $7 billion compensation claim against the joint owners of Samarco.

Samarco, of course, is the owner and operator of the iron ore complex whose tailing dam collapsed on November 5 last year, killing 17 people, swamping nearby communities and causing what is described now as Brazil's biggest environmental disaster.

While the cause of the accident remains uncertain, and the harm it has caused sits a stain on the reputations of all concerned, the crisis mitigation triggered by the collapse of the Fundao dam is a tribute to Samarco management, its employees and its shareholders.

But, over recent weeks, AFR Weekend has been contacted with some vivid criticism of BHP's still-evolving response to the disaster.

"Andrew's visit went down well in the press but was so rushed he didn't even make the time to go to Brasilia to meet the president and their key ministries," one observer told AFR Weekend. "And no one has missed the fact that he has not been back since."

"The whole [BHP] approach," according to an internal critic, "is that this is technical engineering problem, not a complex and dynamic social, political, reputational problem".

Another source close to the matter, and speaking on the promise of anonymity, said: "The discussion with the government is absolute chaos. Neither the government nor the companies have a clear plan.

"BHP and Vale do not have a negotiating strategy … or a clear sense of what outcome they are willing to accept. It makes for a very difficult discussion. The government told the companies to come up with a solution. But it did not happen, so they lost patience and started pushing themselves."

While admitting that it has been fully challenged by the multidimensional challenge of this deadly calamity on the edges of its operational world, BHP management bluntly rejects each and all of these claims.

"Any narrative that underplayed the depth of our commitment would be incredibly unfair," BHP public affairs boss Tony Cudmore said on Friday. "From day one, we absolutely understood this was humanitarian crisis and that we would need to resolve a range of social, political and reputational issues."

Claims of chaos and ill-focus are rejected with equal certainty by the man now fully responsible for engineering BHP's short- and long-term response to the disaster, chief commercial officer Dean Della Vale.

"The process with government is relatively new," Della Vale told the Financial Review from Brasilia. "To think that something this complicated is going to be resolved in a linear, mechanical way in a week and a half is just nonsense."

Della Vale characterised this week's talks as a "scoping" exercise rather than a negotiation, and said BHP welcomed Brazil President Dilma Rousseff's intervention in the compensation issue.

"The president has realised if this gets dragged down into a myriad of small claims across all the possible jurisdictions, then this will be a very complex settlement and it will take a long time," he said.

The fact that Della Vale is in Brazil in the first place announces the weighting that Mackenzie and his board have assigned to mitigation of the Samarco matter. After eyeballing the human and environmental toll of Fundao's collapse, Mackenzie told Della Vale to fully delegate the responsibilities of his title and focus full-time on management of BHP's share of Samarco's crisis.

To be clear on what that means in a BHP context, Della Vale sits among the most senior echelon of BHP management. He is a member of the group general management committee, sits among those who could inherit Mackenzie's crown, and his management purview is vast and fundamental to the business.

Della Vale is now deep in the process of relocating to Brazil and he has arrived to a new "president" of the Samarco joint venture, long-time BHP operator Bryan Quinn, and a new country director, Flavio Bulcao. The intention is, quite plainly, to introduce BHP management disciplines to what was a pretty distant outpost of the empire. Della Vale's currently 30-strong local team has also been buttressed by other key Melbourne imports, including long-time sustainability guru Ian Wood and a more recent arrival, government relations boss David Byers. Both, like Della Vale, have been seconded to the Brazilian effort for the duration and they will all be based in Rio, if only because that is the management epicentre of its partner in disaster, Vale.

It is informative, I think, that one fulcrum for the agitation directed to the Financial Review is a failed attempt two weeks ago by BHP's chairman, Jac Nasser, to visit the disaster site in the province of Minas Gerais.

Nasser and fellow director John Schubert made their way to the local capital of Belo Horizonte in a private jet, but poor weather prevented helicopter flight planned to take them to the site. The back-up plan, driving to the site, was rejected and the pair flew back to Rio de Janeiro.

This was apparently received poorly by the locals. "How is that for interest, commitment and respect?" one asked.

Della Vale's proposition is that the directors' retreat reflected only BHP's operational disciplines. That it could have been received as a slight patently boggles him.

"With Jac, you know, it was actually very good that he took time to go and have a look at the site first hand," Della Vale observed. "But safety is paramount in these situations. You don't start stretching systems just to meet schedules. So yes, there was a back up plan. But it is a six-hour-plus return trip to the site [from Belo Horizonte] over wet, foggy roads. The risk/reward was not there. It [the decision not to travel] was done purely on a risk basis. It was nothing more than that. Purely risk. It would have been negligent to do anything else."

It seems everyone has a lot to learn here.

HEADLINE: Clinton's drabness shapes this race
INTRO: An overlooked factor in a bizarre and worrying US presidential race is the uninspiring nature of Democrat front runner Hilary Clinton.
TEXT:
An overlooked factor in a bizarre and worrying US presidential race is the uninspiring nature of Democrat front runner Hilary Clinton.

The month was October and the year 2007; the place, a basketball stadium in Des Moines, Iowa. Gathered were the candidates for the Democratic nomination for presidency of the United States of America.

Among those present were the putative front runner, Hillary Clinton, senator from New York, and her opponents, including senators Joe Biden, now vice president; John Edwards, who had been John Kerry's running mate in 2004; and a relative unknown from Illinois, Barack Obama.

The occasion was a signature event of the Democratic calendar - the Jefferson-Jackson dinner - where candidates lay out their wares before the first nominating event of a presidential cycle, the Iowa caucuses early in the following year.

I was in the hall that night as correspondent for The Australian Financial Review to witness something that has stuck with me ever since, a lesson in American politics that tells you that anything and everything is possible, or as Bill Clinton himself might have said - and did say - "it is not over until last dog dies".

That was the night the front runner blew it with a wooden and confected speech, one of those hectoring speeches that you hope will come quickly to a conclusion. By contrast, the young pretender from Illinois gave a cracker of a speech - before people had tired of Obama performance art - and the rest, as they say, is history.

Looking towards the stage that evening, the one persistent memory is of a forlorn Hillary Clinton - no sign of Bill - at the end of it all dancing listlessly by herself to the strains of The Grateful Dead while the Democratic establishment, led by House speaker Nancy Pelosi, rushed to congratulate Obama.

You almost felt sorry for Clinton, until you reminded yourself that here was a woman who had all the advantages of name recognition and gender in a party looking for an opportunity to nominate the first female president of the United States. She also had money, lots of it.

Obama beat her on the simple proposition that he was a cleanskin. He represented "change you can believe in" - he was not the representative of tawdry, old-style politics that lacked authenticity.

Fast-forward eight years. Hillary Clinton is once more the front runner going into the Iowa caucuses this Monday American time, and in place of a lithe black man she is facing a rumpled 74-year-old democratic socialist from Vermont who speaks with a thick Brooklyn accent.

Bernie Sanders could hardly be less like Obama, yet Clinton is having enormous difficulty putting him away for the simple reason that significant numbers of Democratic voters, especially young people, neither like, nor trust her.

What this tells you is that while Clinton remains the clear favourite to secure the Democratic nomination, the nominating process may yet yield its surprises. Sanders might win on Monday and go on to prevail in the New Hampshire primaries a week or so later, at which point all the submerged questions about Clinton's electability will come welling to the surface.

And who knows? At that point former New York mayor Michael Bloomberg might decide to run as an independent candidate, vastly complicating the Democratic race.

No less intriguing are the permutations on the Republican side, where the front runner Donald Trump continues to defy predictions that sooner or later, his candidacy would crash and burn, or that his hair would catch on fire, or some other misfortune would befall him.

In an American election season like few others, Trump may well defy conventional Republican wisdom which is that in the end "the party decides", a reference to a 2008 study by political scientists that when push comes to shove, the party establishment rallies behind a consensus candidate.

In the midst of what even right-wing commentators are describing as a Republican "crack-up", the party establishment may prove incapable of deciding, in which case anything and everything is possible, including a Trump candidacy. Trump versus Clinton with the possibility of an independent Bloomberg run cannot be ruled out.

Speaking of conventional wisdom from the perspective of a friend and ally, we tend to believe Americans always do the right thing when they have exhausted the other possibilities, to paraphrase Churchill.

On the other hand, we might remind ourselves of the journalist H.L. Mencken's observation that "no one ever went broke underestimating the taste of the American public".

HEADLINE: Tax reform versus tax and spend
INTRO: Parliament resumes this week, but already the battle lines for an election fought on tax and spending are being drawn. On Thursday, The Australian Financial Review urged the government to take personal income tax cuts to this year's election to sharpen incentives to work, save and invest. It will be paid for by raising the GST on household spending. This will require a sophisticated political message that resonates in the suburbs, emphasising the burdensome nature of our tax system and why it is ill-equipped to encourage the economic growth that delivers jobs and higher pay for Australian workers.
TEXT:
Parliament resumes this week, but already the battle lines for an election fought on tax and spending are being drawn. On Thursday, The Australian Financial Review urged the government to take personal income tax cuts to this year's election to sharpen incentives to work, save and invest. It will be paid for by raising the GST on household spending. This will require a sophisticated political message that resonates in the suburbs, emphasising the burdensome nature of our tax system and why it is ill-equipped to encourage the economic growth that delivers jobs and higher pay for Australian workers.

Treasurer Scott Morrison is formulating a tax reform package that would shift the burden of taxation from earning income to spending it. Lifting the GST from 10 per cent to 15 per cent while cutting personal and company incomes taxes would generate a growth dividend, because taxing income blunts incentives more than does taxing consumption. The Treasurer's eventual package most likely would cut back some superannuation tax concessions. If the government was braver than it is, it could tackle some of the exemptions - for health, education and fresh food - that have reduced the GST coverage from 56 to 47 per cent of overall consumption. This could be done while compensating low income-earners who spend more of their income on items that would become more expensive under a higher GST. But the alternative of confiscating more of what ordinary wage earners take home through bracket creep would be just as regressive.

In contrast, Labor's tax and spend package will be based first and foremost on scaremongering on the GST increase in order to distract from the government's income tax cuts. And it will spend more taxpayers' money. This week, Bill Shorten pledged another $4.5 billion for education in 2018 and 2019, mistaking a bucket of money for good policy. Labor suggests that cash is the panacea for fixing education, not well-documented factors like teacher quality. So, even as government's debt interest payments rise above $1 billion a month, Labor wants to spend more. It has no genuine tax reform plan. Instead, Mr Shorten spent January making cringeworthy pitstops in supermarkets to rail against the GST. Now higher taxes on cigarettes supposedly will fund education, again using a temporary revenue boost to fund permanent spending. Tax-dodging multinational corporations will be cracked down on. A small number of wealthy superannuation funds will be taxed more highly (but eligibility for the aged pension will not be tightened). In short, Labor is acting as if the commodities boom is still rollicking along.

But it's not. And as falling national income hits boomtime spending promises, the size of the federal government is rising back to the 26 per cent of GDP it hit during the Rudd spendathon of the global financial crisis. That's up from 23 per cent at the end of the Howard era and a mere 18 per cent before the Whitlam government. As Treasury secretary John Fraser noted on Thursday, this spending-to-GDP ratio has increased above 25 per cent only four times since 1970s and only previously during economic downturns. If spending stays this high, he notes, taxes would have to be lifted "very substantially" to close the budget deficit. But simply trying to increase the overall tax burden actually would not work, Mr Fraser adds, because that would blunt incentives and hurt investment, growth and job creation - and so shrink the tax base.

The Turnbull government regrettably has allowed the timetable for returning to even a sliver of budget surplus to slip into the next decade. That just highlights how the current spending track is untenable, permanently inflated by a temporary income bonanza, even before boomtime initiatives such as the National Disability Insurance Scheme are rolled in. But while the government might lack urgency, what is Labor's answer? Depressingly, it seems to be to raise taxes and spend it all.

HEADLINE: Emirates offers world's longest flight
INTRO: Emirates will launch the first non-stop flights between Auckland and Dubai from March 2, in a move that will give it a brief crown as the longest flight in the world and effectively increase the capacity available for bookings on its trans-Tasman joint venture with Qantas.
TEXT:
Emirates will launch the first non-stop flights between Auckland and Dubai from March 2, in a move that will give it a brief crown as the longest flight in the world and effectively increase the capacity available for bookings on its trans-Tasman joint venture with Qantas.

Emirates will maintain its current trans-Tasman schedule of three A380 and one Boeing 777-300ER flights a day, despite adding five weekly non-stop services between Auckland and Dubai on a 777-200LR. The Auckland-Dubai sector will rank ahead of Qantas' Dallas-Sydney flight as the longest in the world in distance and will have a flying time of 17 hours and 15 minutes.

However, there is plenty of competition for the crown of the world's longest flight. Emirates has announced plans to fly 17 hours and 35 minutes non-stop from Dubai to Panama City on March 31 and Qatar Airways chief executive Akbar Al Baker reportedly said this week his airline was interested in launching non-stop flights from Doha to Auckland later in 2016.

Singapore Airlines plans to resume nearly 19-hour non-stop flights between Singapore and New York from 2018 and United Airlines announced on Friday plans for non-stop San Francisco-Singapore services, with a flying time of 16 hours and 20 minutes.

Emirates' decision to announce the new route just a month before the first flights is unusual, and industry sources said it was probably part of an effort to beat rival Qatar to the market. Emirates said travellers booked on its existing services to Dubai and beyond via Australia would be able to switch to the new flight without additional fees, subject to seat availability. That will mean more trans-Tasman seats in the coming months.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission required Qantas and Emirates to maintain a minimum level of trans-Tasman capacity as part of their joint venture approved in 2013, which allows the airlines to co-ordinate pricing and scheduling.

Emirates has improved its load factor, or the percentage of seats filled, on trans-Tasman flights through its relationship with Qantas. In October 2012 Emirates filled about 69 per cent of trans-Tasman seats but that increased to 75 per cent by October 2015. However, in October 2015 the Emirates load remained lower than Air New Zealand with 86 per cent, Qantas at 84 per cent, Virgin at 83 per cent and Jetstar at 81 per cent.

A Qantas spokesman said New Zealand has always been "central to the success" of its Emirates partnership, with the carriers combined contributing about 32,000 seats a week on trans-Tasman routes.

"We know that our customers like the range of routes and aircraft types available with Qantas and Emirates," he said. "We expect that most Qantas and Emirates customers who fly to New Zealand will continue to travel via Australia, but this new route will supplement those existing services and provide an option that wasn't available before."

Auckland Airport estimated the new non-stop Auckland-Dubai flights would provide an extra 194,180 seats a year on the Dubai route. The 777-200LR aircraft has 266 seats, include eight first class suites, 42 lie-flat business class seats and 216 economy class seats in a 3-4-3 configuration.

Before the Emirates announcement was made, First NZ Capital estimated trans-Tasman capacity would rise 8.1 per cent in the financial year starting July 1 as other carriers enter the competitive market.

Air New Zealand shares were trading 5.3 per cent lower at $2.60 at 12.15pm AEDT on Friday, while Qantas shares were trading 2 per cent higher at $3.90.
